 Market Intelligence: Advisor Legal Research Market Data City of Chicago, IL Chicago CFO's exit raises disclosure concerns 
 By Jennifer Shea Published November 16, 2026, 5:22 p.m. EST | Updated November 16, 2026, 5:31 p.m. EST 9 Min Read Facebook 
 Twitter 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 The exit of Chicago CFO Ashlee Gabrysch has heightened tensions between the city council and Mayor Brandon Johnson's administration. Bloomberg News What's at stake: Amid budget conflict and as some of its bond ratings hover just above junk, Chicago needs to reassure the market.
 Supporting data: Gabrysch is the fifth Chicago finance or budget leader to quit this year.
 Forward look: There are less than 50 days left before the city must pass its 2027 budget.
 Processing Content Twelve aldermen on Chicago's finance committee called on Monday for an independent review of the city's finances and financial reporting over the past three years, saying they have concerns about "the accuracy and transparency of financial information presented by the administration."
 After Chicago CFO Ashlee Gabrysch quit on Friday , aldermen scrambled to sort out what happened following insinuations from Gabrysch and recriminations from the administration of Mayor Brandon Johnson, which initially threatened to refer Gabrysch to Chicago's Office of Inspector General.
 "In the wake of last week's resignation of the city's third CFO in a year, we find ourselves at a moment where every effort must be made to secure the public's confidence in our city's finances," Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell said in a statement Monday announcing the ordinance authorizing the review. "We must ensure the reliability of these statements associated with the city's financial condition, revenues, expenditures, and other obligations." 
 Gabrysch is the fifth finance or budget leader to leave the Johnson administration this year. Former CFO Jill Jaworski left to take a job with Navy Pier in January. This summer, Deputy CFO Noor Shaikh and acting CFO Steven Mahr both left their posts , followed closely by Budget Director Annette Guzman . 
 Gabrysch, a veteran of Fitch Ratings, the Cook County CFO's office and the Civic Federation, was hired as CFO in August; she lasted almost exactly three months before abruptly resigning on Friday.
 Mohammed Murad, head of municipal credit research at PT Asset Management, nodded to a line from a James Bond novel : "Once is a fluke. Twice is coincidence. Three times is a pattern."
 "I think that's right where we are now," he said by email. "The market already knows about the city's financial challenges, and they aren't exactly new, either, but personnel turnover in key positions is what is new."
 This weekend's developments may increase the city's cost of borrowing, he said. "It is the ongoing political and fiscal instability that is getting in the way of a lasting fix that the city needs. Right now, it feels like the market may have to look past this administration's term and wait until 2027 for any real progress" on the fiscal front.
 The mayor is up for reelection in February, with a crowded field of challengers.
 "Turnover in that role is not a good thing, and there's been a lot of it," said Tim McGregor, managing partner at Riverbend Capital Advisors. "I thought Jill Jaworski was doing a good job and I thought she had a pretty good plan. Her departure was a bad indicator for the city," which is "getting caught back in some of the old problems now."
 Gabrysch's resignation comes on the heels of a letter signed by a majority of aldermen rejecting about $400 million of revenue in the mayor's proposed budget, noted Scott Nees, director of U.S. public finance at S&P Global Ratings.
 "In the weeks ahead, we will be focusing on budget negotiations as the city council and mayor seek to close an $882 million budget gap, and we will be interested in understanding if additional credit-relevant information comes to light regarding the CFO's resignation," Nees said by email. 
 "With only a little over six weeks left before the Dec. 31 deadline for passing a new budget, the leadership vacuum could not have come at a more critical moment," he added. "At minimum, we believe the absence of a CFO during the coming weeks' budget negotiations makes a constructive outcome — for example, a budget passed on time with meaningful progress reducing the structural fiscal deficit — less certain."
 City Comptroller Michael Belsky was named as interim CFO, according to the mayor's office.
 Chicago's general obligation bonds are rated BBB-plus by Fitch Ratings and KBRA and BBB by S&P Global Ratings, with negative outlooks, and Baa3 with a stable outlook by Moody's Ratings.
 In a statement she issued upon her resignation, Gabrysch cited her commitment to financial integrity and transparency and said "that to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations."
 The mayor's critics said her statement pointed to serious concerns about the way the administration conducts its budget process — and whether its numbers can be relied on.
 Alderman Scott Waguespack pointed to a Securities and Exchange Commission case in Miami in 2013, in which the SEC charged the city and its former budget director with securities fraud tied to municipal bond offerings and disclosures made to bond investors.
 Miami ultimately paid $1 million in 2016 to settle charges the city acted fraudulently in taking steps to hide its deteriorating financial condition from bondholders.
 "They made misleading statements to investors, and there was an SEC complaint," Waguespack said. "I was told that it's potentially the same thing" at issue in Chicago now.
 The Miami charges involved misleading statements and omissions around interfund transfers in three 2009 bond deals and in the city's annual comprehensive financial reports for 2007 and 2008. The transfers served to mask growing deficits in the city's operating fund as the city marketed bonds. 
 Waguespack noted that acting Budget Director Jonathan Ernst has been on medical leave since the day after the first budget session, and "during the budget hearings, we were asking for a lot of information that we're still waiting on," he said. "This has been going on for at least a year before we got to it, but this is the kind of lack of information sharing that's happening."
 He pointed to a meeting shortly before Gabrysch publicly said the budget is not 76% structurally balanced, at which the mayor, the CFO, the budget director and Belsky were present.
 Waguespack said "the political people in the mayor's office jumped in" to override Gabrysch. "We just weren't sure what was happening there," he said. "We just want transparency and accountability on who's making the decisions."
 He said aldermen were taken aback when the mayor's office threatened to refer Gabrysch to the OIG for making a $75 million extra pension payment the city council approved with a veto-proof majority.
 "She actually had the authority to make that payment," he said. "To turn around and blame her for something like that was just ridiculous... The IG is a former SEC guy. Maybe they forgot that. That's not the kind of guy you want to play games with."
 A spokesperson for the city's finance team did not respond to questions by press time.
 The disclosure rumblings, if proven true, would be "a big deal," said Justin Marlowe, research professor at the University of Chicago's Harris School of Public Finance and director of the Center for Municipal Finance.
 "Securities disclosure is very serious, and the SEC has investigated this in some other cases and brought cases against public officials who were found to have made material misstatements," he said. "It's not something that happens often, but when it has happened, it's gotten a lot of attention. So again, without suggesting that's what happened here, that is something that the market takes very seriously."
 Lisa Washburn, chief credit officer and managing director at Municipal Market Analytics, said that while she can't speak to what happened behind the scenes, "the idea that there may have been either an intent to mislead, or an intent to make the financial picture look better than it was, is concerning."
 She added, "Ashlee is a well-known and respected member of the municipal finance community, and so any sort of attack on her character, if it's unfounded, it certainly doesn't provide confidence in the fiscal management coming from the mayor's office."
 There is clearly a substantive dispute at the heart of Gabrysch's resignation, Marlowe said. 
 "Part of the problem is framing this question of exactly how much does the mayor's proposed budget depend on structural versus one-time solutions?" he said. "That might seem like a wonky difference… but it is a substantive difference, especially given that the rating agencies have been very upfront about Chicago needing to move away from one-time solutions and toward structural solutions."
 The mayor is "entitled to tell the story that he wants to tell," Marlowe said. But Gabrysch's views on the city's credit were well known when she was hired , and she was hired in part for the respect she and her views carried within the finance community.
 "This is what CFOs do if they feel like they can't advance the narrative that they think is truest to their view of the financial reality," he said. "They resign."
 What Gabrysch herself has shared publicly is enough to warrant serious concern, Alderman Bill Conway said.
 "The former CFO implied that the mayor's office asked her to provide false information about our finances, either to credit agencies or to city council, and that's the type of thing that warrants a full investigation," Conway told The Bond Buyer. 
 He pointed to an op-ed by Gabrysch published this weekend and to her testimony before city council, "where she was asked how much of the reduction of the deficit is due to structural change, and she said the number was 56%, not the 76% that the administration had implied," Conway said.
 "The mayor said 76% of this year's budget fix is 'structural,' meaning it solves the problem for good, rather than for one year. That's only true if you leave out the money the city is borrowing to pay legal settlements, about a quarter of the total fix. When I testified, I counted that borrowing. I still do," Gabrysch wrote in the op-ed.
 "That itself is a shocking act against taxpayers," Conway said. "But if you look beyond that, how often has this administration asked others to falsify financial information?"
 Howard Cure, partner and director of municipal bond research at Evercore Wealth Management, said this dustup over math seems unnecessary because it's "not (like) this is some kind of state secret, as far as the fact that the budget is not structurally balanced. We've been talking about this for years. Every budget," he said. 
 The city's audited financial reporting is up to date, with the most recent report landing six months after the previous fiscal year closed.
 "I don't know (what) made (Gabrysch) so uncomfortable, but it's pretty disquieting and concerning when you have a CFO start mentioning that what she was asked to do goes against her principles," Cure said.
 Joe Ferguson, president of the Civic Federation, a Chicago-based fiscal watchdog group, in a Friday statement called Gabrysch's exit "an extremely unsettling and destabilizing event at a time when the city's credit rating sits on the brink of junk status. 
 "The only response is transparency and oversight," Ferguson said. "The Civic Federation is calling for an independent investigation into the former CFO's allegations and an immediate special oversight hearing" by the finance committee into Gabrysch's allegation of a breach of fiduciary duty.
 David Skeel, a professor of corporate law at the University of Pennsylvania and veteran of the Puerto Rico bankruptcy oversight and management board, tweeted this weekend , "It sure does seem as though the foundations are shaking in Chicago."
 "I think the credit pressure will remain and pick up," McGregor said. The city now faces "a long, long road that's going to take more structural change than a specific short-term solution," he said.
 All the turnover, and the allegations surrounding Gabrysch's departure, are "troubling from an investor's point of view," Cure said. "City Council is going to become more and more assertive… (Johnson is) giving them little choice but to assert themselves even more."
